nodes.description: The favoured embryological model places the primary error at the caudal end of the developing notochord at about Carnegie stage 7 (16 days after ovulation), in the tail bud from which notochord, neural tube, somites and hindgut all arise. A caudal notochord defect is thought to disturb the separation of ventral gut endoderm from dorsal neuroectoderm, leaving abnormal connections between them, and to derange secondary neurulation and formation of the sacral vertebrae. The model explains why anorectal, sacral, presacral and spinal anomalies occur together, but it is inferred from the anatomy of the malformations rather than observed.

nodes.description: Surgery is the main treatment. The presacral mass is excised, the anorectal malformation is corrected, usually through a posterior sagittal approach, and the dysraphic spinal anomalies are repaired with untethering of the cord. These can be done in a single combined neurosurgical and general surgical operation, in which the spinal canal is opened through a midline laminoplasty and the incision extended to a posterior sagittal approach to the presacral mass; this approach has been reported without recurrence, retethering or cerebrospinal fluid fistula. Early resection is advised because of the risks of infection, meningitis and malignant transformation of an undiagnosed presacral mass. Constipation and neurogenic bladder dysfunction often persist afterwards. A neonate presenting with obstruction may first need a colostomy, with the definitive operation staged later. Anal stenosis in this syndrome responds poorly to dilatation alone.
